<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discrete Flow Matching and Stochastic Interpolants</h5>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Developed in quick succession by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Campbell et al. (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gat et al. (2024)</a></cite>, Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) extends the generative framework of continuous Flow Matching (FM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> to discrete and general probability spaces. For DFM as for FM, the training objective is to learn the velocity field (used for sampling) which generates a probability path that interpolates between coupled distributions, most commonly between noise (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>) and data (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{data}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>data</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{data}}</annotation></semantics></math>). Unlike the time-dependent continuous velocity vector field in Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, the velocity field for DFM is presented as the time-dependent rate matrix within a Continuous Time Markov Chain (CTMC) realization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Campbell et al., 2024</a>)</cite> which transports samples through a continuum of marginal distributions <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,1]}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,1]}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t=1}=p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t=1}=p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Connected to the rate matrix by the Kolmogorov Forward Equation (KFE), these marginals bridge <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> in finite time and form a stochastic process formalized as stochastic interpolants by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Albergo et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diffusion with Learnable Noise</h5>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The standard diffusion approach from DDPM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite> uses an isotropic Gaussian noising kernel for the forward process, which gives a closed-form expression for the marginal and guarantees that the functional form of the learnable posterior is likewise an isotropic Gaussian. Despite the simple and effective formulation, the reverse noising process is independent over positions and has no explicit mechanism by which to coordinate denoising decisions among positions or pixels. Moving away from standard Gaussian noising, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al. (2023)</a></cite> show that the generative abilities of image diffusion models are not strongly dependent on the the corruption process, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daras et al. (2022)</a></cite> learn the score function for any linear corruption process. Both <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rissanen et al. (2022)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoogeboom &amp; Salimans (2022)</a></cite> introduce diffusion based on blurring or heat dissipation, where the noise process destroys low-information regions faster than high-information ones, thus instilling a coarse-to-fine inductive bias into the generative process. <span id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MuLAN</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sahoo et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> also introduces a multivariate per-position <span id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">learned</span> noise schedule, tightening the variational ELBO and allowing diffusion to denoise different spatial regions at different rates. Even more recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bartosh et al. (2024)</a></cite> propose Neural Flow Diffusion Models (NFDM) which defines the forward process’ conditional SDE via a learnable parametric transformation and enables the specification of a variety of data- and time-dependent noising processes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Similarly to image diffusion, the prevailing framework in widely-adopted masked diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sahoo et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> relies on the reversal of a non-parametric masking schedule that is independent and uniform across positions. However, this paradigm does not take into account the potential value of learning which token positions to decode in what order. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite> take up this question of token generation ordering.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Variable Length Discrete Flow Matching</h5>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The useful desiderata of <span id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i)</span> modeling distributions over variable-length sequences and <span id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii)</span> the ability to insert tokens have inspired a number of recent works to move away from fixed-window text diffusion towards insertion- and substitution- based discrete flow models in which positions during the generation process acquire a relative rather than absolute interpretation. In particular, FlexMDM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> grows a sequence by parameterizing an action space which allows the insertion of a mask token and the unmasking of already-inserted masks. Concurrently with FlexMDM, EditFlows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Havasi et al., 2025</a>)</cite> defines a discrete flow by means of insertion, deletion and substitution operations to support variable-length sequence generation. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patel et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> proposes insertion language modeling (ILM) which allows the direct insertions of unmasked tokens, as opposed to the two-step insertion/unmasking approach of FlexMDM.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
